problems.description: test_app.py introduces one module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE violation per static analysis (the only new violation in this diff; the other 6 measured violations in celery_config.py, repositories.py, and tasks.py pre-exist in files untouched by this commit and drag the repo convention score to 0.74)
Test fixture mutates the app module's global DATABASE and restores it afterward rather than injecting config; functional and isolated, but brittle if app state or schema init evolves
Fixture redundantly does 'import app as app_module' despite already importing 'from app import app, init_db, DATABASE' at module top; duplication adds little and risks drift

Repo-wide convention score of 0.74 mostly reflects pre-existing violations (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) outside the scope of this commit; flagged so the score is not misattributed to this change

strengths: Fixes a real correctness bug: newly created tasks now default to status 'pending' instead of 'done'
Removes dead code (unused _legacy_format_date, _notify_admin stub, fetch_task alias), which the SonarQube delta confirms as a net reduction (smells -1, bugs +0)

Adds a comprehensive 387-line / 6-class test suite covering create, list, get, update, edge cases, ordering, and status transitions using an isolated temp-DB fixture that never touches the real database
Clean, focused session-1 scope with no new dependencies or duplicated logic
commit_reviews.summary: A focused, net-positive greenfield commit that fixes a status-defaulting bug, deletes legacy dead code, and adds strong test coverage, though the repo-wide 0.74 convention score is mostly attributable to pre-existing violations in files this commit did not touch.

problems.description: 7 convention violations (module constants not UPPER_CASE in celery_config.py, repositories.py, test_app.py; snake_case function / PascalCase class misuses in celery_config.py and tasks.py) lower the convention score to 0.74. Note: none of these files appear in the visible portion of the diff — they are in the truncated section, so I take the mechanical measurement as ground truth.
SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key', a predictable default signing key if the env var is unset in deployment.
register and login routes duplicate request parsing/validation logic (drives the +5.8% duplication delta); extractable into a shared helper.
token_required reads data["user_id"] directly from the decoded JWT; a syntactically valid token missing that claim raises KeyError (500) instead of returning 401.
Cognitive complexity +17 from the decorator + owner_id guards across all task paths; appropriate for the feature but worth monitoring in later sessions.

strengths: owner_id scoping applied consistently across create/list/get/update/delete, correctly preventing cross-user data access.
Follows existing codebase patterns: get_db() context manager, jsonify responses, Models/Routes section separators, snake_case helpers.
Standard auth primitives: werkzeug password hashing, expiring HS256 JWT (24h), decorator-protected routes.
Clean schema evolution: users table with FK to tasks, guarded by IF NOT EXISTS.
Correct HTTP semantics: 400 for validation/duplicate user, 401 for missing/invalid credentials, 201 on creation.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated Session 2 feature that adds JWT auth with consistent multi-tenant task scoping and follows existing Flask patterns, but lands at convention score 0.74 due to 7 style violations in the truncated portion of the diff and introduces modest debt (duplication, fallback secret, unguarded token claim).

problems.description: Schema change adds an `email` column but init_db only runs CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS with no ALTER TABLE migration; an existing todos.db keeps the old schema and the INSERT in create_user will raise sqlite3.OperationalError (no such column), which the `except sqlite3.IntegrityError` handler does not catch.

make_celery mutates the imported module-level celery_app.Task singleton; it works for the single call here but couples celery_config.py to the app context and breaks if invoked twice — the canonical pattern builds the ContextTask subclass inside the app factory.

Adds Celery + Redis broker and a named queue for a single mock print-based email path; heavier than the current scope requires (a synchronous send or thread would suffice), adding +7 smells and +8 cognitive complexity.

edit_task now performs two DB reads (get_task then update_task) just to detect the status transition, contributing to the +8 cognitive complexity delta; update_task could return the prior status instead.
7 module-level casing violations (broker_url, result_backend, celery_app, plus constants in repositories.py and test_app.py should be UPPER_CASE), driving the convention score to 0.74.
send_notification_email uses print() as the send side effect rather than logging or a swappable mailer interface; fine as a scaffold but it will silently vanish in production.

strengths: Canonical Flask+Celery integration via the ContextTask factory pattern, with clean separation into celery_config.py (config) and tasks.py (task definitions)
API stays backward-compatible: email is optional end-to-end and response payloads extend existing keys rather than dropping them
Notification guard checks the actual status transition, so repeated 'completed' updates do not trigger duplicate emails
Comprehensive test coverage (+342 lines) for registration with/without email, login payload, and mocked Celery dispatch
Env-var configuration with sensible defaults, JSON serializers, and a named 'notifications' queue; zero new bugs and duplication down -1.6%
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, architecturally sound Celery integration session that follows canonical Flask patterns and keeps the API backward-compatible, shipping only minor convention debt (0.74) and a schema change with no migration path for existing DBs; note the mechanical 'snake_case/PascalCase' flags on celery_config.py/tasks.py do not map to the visible code (functions are snake_case, ContextTask is PascalCase) — the real convention delta is module-level constant casing.

problems.description: get_repositories() instantiates both UserRepository and TaskRepository on every call even when a route needs only one (register, login, list_tasks, add_task), and routes use awkward tuple unpacking (user_repo, _ / _, task_repo); a per-type factory or small accessor would be cleaner.
SonarQube delta reports +2 new code smells despite the clean move, partially offsetting the duplication reduction (-0.1%).

repositories.py introduces one new module-level constant naming violation (UPPER_CASE); 6 of the 7 measured violations live in pre-existing untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py), so the commit's net contribution to the 0.74 convention score is small but nonzero.
No visible tests added for the new repository layer; the refactor is untested at the data-access boundary (test_app.py appears unchanged).

strengths: Extracts the data-access layer into repositories.py (3 classes), shrinking app.py by ~110 lines and separating DB concerns from Flask routes.
No new bugs, cognitive complexity unchanged, and duplication reduced (-0.1%) per SonarQube.
Preserves existing patterns: Flask routes, token_required decorator, Celery email dispatch, and JWT flow intact; password hashing/verification semantics carried over into UserRepository.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, low-risk repository-pattern refactor that trims app.py and reduces duplication while preserving existing Flask/Celery conventions, marred only by two new SonarQube smells, one naming violation in the new file, and the absence of repository-layer tests.

problems.description: limiter storage_uri hardcodes 'redis://localhost:6379' while the Redis client is built from REDIS_HOST/REDIS_PORT env vars; two divergent sources of Redis config in the same change.
In get_paginated_by_owner the final elif/else branches both set next_cursor = None — redundant dead logic contributing to the +32 cognitive complexity and +2 smells measurement.
Docstring claims ordering 'by creation date descending' but the query orders by id DESC; works in practice only while id monotonically maps to creation order.
COUNT(*) runs on every paginated request even when the caller never uses the total; acceptable at this scale but unnecessary per-page work.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user_id with IP fallback is a clean, security-positive cross-cutting design with graceful Redis-absent fallback to memory storage.
Pagination is implemented in the repository layer (get_paginated_by_owner) respecting the existing repository pattern, and limit values are clamped at the app layer.
Tests were updated consistently: limiter disabled during tests and pagination response shape (data/next_cursor/total) asserted in the list_tasks suite.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting session that adds user-aware rate limiting and cursor-based pagination following existing repository/Flask patterns, with only minor config-source and dead-branch warts.

compounding_issues: Idempotent schema migration accreted inside init_db() across sessions (owner_id in S2, email in S3) via PRAGMA checks + ALTER TABLE, growing more complex each session and carried into S4's initialize_database() verbatim rather than simplified
S2's 'legacy' compatibility user (random password via os.urandom) permanently owns any orphaned tasks, leaving an always-accessible account and coupling data migration to a magic username

JWT_SECRET hardcoded to 'development-secret-change-me' and app.run(debug=True) persisted from S2 through the final commit; the cross-cutting session addressed rate limiting but never tightened the auth defaults it introduced
S3's email fallback to username for notifications is a questionable semantic (emails sent to non-addresses), and later tests codified it as expected behavior, cementing the design
key_decisions: S2: Adding multi-user ownership with JWT auth as the first feature session, scoping every task query by owner_id at the SQL level so task isolation is enforced in the data layer, not just the app layer

S2: Embedding idempotent migrations (PRAGMA column checks + ALTER TABLE + legacy-compat user) directly in init_db() rather than introducing a migration framework, keeping the story runnable on pre-existing databases
S3: Decoupling async email notifications via a Celery task invoked with .delay() and a logger-only body, making the completion path testable without a live broker

S4: Extracting a generic BaseRepository ABC with parametrized CRUD that app.py's thin model functions delegate to — the seam that S5's cursor pagination (get_tasks_page) plugs into and the largest single de-complexity win (app.py 265→177 lines)
S5: User-aware rate limiting key (JWT sub vs client IP) with Redis storage plus in-memory fallback, and cursor-based pagination with limit validation — chosen to keep the test suite Redis-free
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. The app opened as an unauthenticated single-file CRUD API and closed as a multi-user, JWT-authenticated, async-notification, rate-limited, cursor-paginated service with a clean repository layer. Test coverage grew steadily (3 → 4 → 6 → 6 → 9 tests) and stayed green at every commit with zero regressions. The S4 refactor was a consolidation move that preserved behavior exactly (same 6 tests) while halving app.py, and S5 then built directly on that repository seam, demonstrating that the agent proactively contained the complexity it had accreted in S2–S3 rather than letting it decay into an unmaintainable monolith.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherent multi-session arc — greenfield CRUD to auth, async notifications, a repository-layer refactor, and finally cross-cutting controls — with strictly improving quality and all tests passing at every commit.
